items.title: [npr.org] Alaska Native villages remain displaced a year after Typhoon Halong
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

A year after the remnants of Typhoon Halong destroyed homes and infrastructure in western Alaska, residents of Kipnuk and Kwigillingok remain displaced as repairs continue, with many unsure when they can return. The October 2025 storm affected more than 40 communities, and about 1,500 people were evacuated from Kwigillingok, Kipnuk and Nightmute. Alaska officials estimate that federal aid will make most Kipnuk homes livable by Thanksgiving, but say some residents need replacement housing. The state is seeking more funding. Both Kipnuk and Kwigillingok voted to relocate to higher ground, but current disaster funding is not designed to pay for moving the communities.

items.title: [al-monitor.com] US sanctions eight Canadian currency firms over alleged Iran transfers
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

The U.S. Treasury on Nov. 6 sanctioned eight money-services businesses in Ontario and British Columbia, alleging they moved funds for Iran and sanctioned Iranian entities, including by converting Iranian rials and other currencies into digital assets. The businesses are Million Exchange, Amin Exchange, Top PC Technician, NIA Nations Currency, Farah Exchange, CCC Inc., Cryptoyal and Darvish Exchange. The sanctions block any assets they hold under U.S. jurisdiction and bar U.S. persons and entities from transacting with them. U.S. officials also said several firms handled money for Ryan Wedding, a Canadian former Olympic snowboarder and alleged drug-trafficking figure. The Treasury accused three firms of laundering drug proceeds by converting bulk cash into digital assets. The action was coordinated with the Financial Transactions and Reports Analysis Centre of Canada (FINTRAC), Canada’s financial intelligence agency, and U.S. agencies. Separately, the Treasury’s Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN), the U.S. anti-money-laundering unit, barred U.S. financial institutions from processing transfers involving MEXC Global, a cryptocurrency exchanger incorporated in Seychelles. FinCEN said MEXC facilitated at least $16 billion in illicit transactions linked to Iran, North Korea and Russia, as well as other sanctioned actors.

items.title: [theguardian.com] France protests draw 320,000 as clashes spread to German cities
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

About 320,000 people protested across France on Saturday, Oct. 31, in a third consecutive weekend of demonstrations over living costs, education and public services; youth groups put turnout closer to 500,000. Most marches were peaceful, but clashes broke out as crowds dispersed in Paris, Lyon, Marseille and Toulouse. Police used tear gas, water cannon and baton charges, and authorities reported more than 560 arrests nationwide. A Molotov cocktail struck a police officer in Paris in what Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez called attempted murder. The movement began with students protesting poor school conditions, teacher shortages and university admissions they say disadvantage poorer applicants, then drew unions and Yellow Vest activists. The government’s turnout estimate fell from 410,000 the previous weekend and 550,000 on Oct. 17, when riots and looting damaged shops and public buildings. Student organizations have called for school and university blockades, while a general strike is expected in the coming days. The GenZ regelt! campaign also organized youth-led protests in 34 German cities over living costs, education funding and compulsory military service. After largely peaceful daytime marches, violence erupted in Frankfurt, where shops were looted and a gun store was among those targeted. Police said they arrested a suspect and seized two weapons. Police also used water cannon or pepper spray in several cities.

items.title: [cw39.com] Researchers favor permanent standard time as US debates clock changes
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

Most U.S. clocks turn back one hour Nov. 1, as new research reviews renew debate over whether year-round standard time or daylight saving time better supports health. A Canadian policy analysis and a review focused on people with mental illness argue that permanent standard time better protects sleep, mood and biological rhythms. A broader review of population studies, however, finds a mix of harms and benefits from seasonal clock changes and summer daylight saving time. Permanent daylight saving time would delay winter sunrise, while permanent standard time would bring earlier summer sunrises and winter sunsets. The U.S. House passed a bill to make daylight saving time permanent in July 2026, but the Senate has not taken it up. The next seasonal clock change is scheduled for March 14, 2027.

items.title: [cbsnews.com] U.S. employers add 165,000 jobs as unemployment falls to 4.1%
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

U.S. employers added 165,000 jobs in October, more than double economists’ forecast of about 65,000, and the unemployment rate fell to 4.1% from 4.2%, the Labor Department reported Nov. 6. The department also revised August and September payroll gains up by a combined 84,000, bringing average monthly job growth over the past three months to 137,000. Professional and business services added 70,000 jobs, health care 42,000, transportation and warehousing 25,000, and manufacturing 19,000. The number of people working part time for economic reasons rose by 339,000 to 4.8 million, while average hourly earnings rose 3.1% over the year, below September’s inflation rate of 3.7%. After the report, investors put the probability of a Federal Reserve rate increase at the Dec. 8-9 meeting at about 77%-80%. The Fed held its benchmark rate at 3.75%-4.00% in October. October consumer-price data are due Tuesday, Nov. 10.

items.title: [sciencefeatured.com] Higher BMI over time linked to faster cognitive decline in older adults
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

A 24-year study of several thousand middle-aged and older Americans found that higher average body mass index (BMI) over time was associated with faster declines in memory and thinking. A team led by University of Georgia researcher Suhang Song reported the findings in the Journal of Neurology. The association was strongest when cognitive abilities were assessed about eight years after weight measurements and was more pronounced among participants who were older when the study began. The observational study cannot establish that higher weight causes cognitive decline or that weight loss would prevent it. The researchers noted that participants reported their own height and weight and that the analysis could not account for physical activity. The team called for further research into possible biological mechanisms and future interventions.

items.title: [jns.org] Trump announces plan to end $3.8 billion in annual U.S. aid to Israel
items.content_html:

President Donald Trump said the United States would end its $3.8 billion in annual military aid to Israel by the end of 2026, saying he and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had agreed to the move months earlier. Trump made the announcement on Nov. 3, as Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress. Israel's current 10-year aid agreement runs through 2028, and officials sought clarity on how an early end would work. Vice President JD Vance cited the Iran war and the U.S. relationship with Israel among factors behind Republicans' midterm losses. The incoming Democratic majority takes office in January 2027 and could scrutinize funding for military operations and assistance, though the outgoing Congress could still act on defense legislation before then. Israel's Oct. 27 election left no bloc with a clear majority. President Isaac Herzog said 67 lawmakers in the 120-seat Knesset recommended opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot to form a government, compared with 46 backing Netanyahu. Herzog said he planned to give a lawmaker the mandate on Sunday, Nov. 8, after further talks.

items.content_html:

Hundreds of civilians evacuated from Russian-occupied Oleshky reached Ukrainian-held territory on Saturday, Oct. 31, after a local ceasefire allowed them to leave and aid to enter. U.S. First Lady Melania Trump mediated the pause, while Pope Leo XIV urged access for aid and evacuations. The ceasefire began Tuesday in the southern Kherson region and was scheduled to end Sunday evening. Residents travelled by bus through occupied Crimea to Russia, then flew to Belarus and crossed into Ukraine’s Chernihiv region, where relatives and aid workers met them. Some evacuees said food supplies had run out and they had survived on garden plants. The ceasefire also allowed roads to be cleared of mines and food and medicine to enter Oleshky. Ukraine and Russia have not disclosed how many people left. Melania Trump said the convoy could safely evacuate more than 750 people; an estimated 1,700 remained in Oleshky before the operation. Russia’s human rights commissioner said both sides had agreed to continue humanitarian missions. The truce was set to expire Sunday night.

items.title: [tagesspiegel.de] Bird flu risk rises as 6,000 turkeys culled in northern Germany
items.content_html:

Germany’s Friedrich Loeffler Institute raised its bird-flu risk ratings for spread among wild birds and entry into poultry farms from “moderate” to “high” as an outbreak led to the culling of about 6,000 turkeys at a farm in Rostock district, Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania. The state said the outbreak at the Wattmannshagen farm was its first poultry-farm case of the season. In Brandenburg, officials confirmed the autumn’s first case in a wild goose in Oder-Spree district. The institute reported that cases in wild birds and poultry had risen since October after a quieter period through September, with bird migration and falling temperatures contributing to the spread. items.content_html:

It linked the unusually warm water to exceptional coastal rainfall, rainfall deficits in the Andean highlands and Amazon, and reduced nutrient levels affecting some fisheries. Officials urged preparations for coastal flooding. Separately, Copernicus reported that the global average sea-surface temperature outside polar regions reached a September record of 21.05°C.

items.title: [proplanta.de] Germany mandates video monitoring at large slaughterhouses handling 90% of animals
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

Germany’s parliament approved mandatory video monitoring at large slaughterhouses on Nov. 5, requiring cameras to record the handling and killing of animals at facilities above specified slaughter thresholds. The law covers about 232 of the country’s roughly 4,000 slaughterhouses, which process around 90% of animals slaughtered in Germany. The rules take effect Jan. 1, 2027, and give affected businesses a year to install the equipment. Authorities may also order monitoring at smaller plants when there are specific grounds to suspect animal-welfare violations. Veterinary authorities can access recordings after slaughter, and the footage may be analyzed using artificial intelligence. Parliament also delayed the planned state animal-husbandry label for meat from Jan. 1, 2027, to Oct. 1, 2027, citing the time needed to reform the system.

The report’s 146 researchers from 30 countries urged governments to treat climate change as a global health emergency and coordinate a sustained response. Extreme rainfall affected 17.2% of global land each year from 2016 to 2025, up from 14.8% in the preceding decade, and the researchers linked shifting groundwater conditions to risks for food security and sanitation. Southeast Asia and Africa suffered the largest productivity-related economic losses, equivalent to 3.9% and 3.2% of gross domestic product, respectively. The report calls for governments to consider health in climate decisions and direct climate and health funding to vulnerable countries. Researchers are expected to press the issue at the COP31 climate conference in Antalya, Türkiye, scheduled for Nov. 9-20.

items.content_html:

AI safety nonprofit Model Evaluation and Threat Research (METR) says Anthropic may have crossed its own early-warning threshold for AI-driven research acceleration as early as July. METR released its review alongside a finding that model capabilities on selected tasks have improved about 1.9 times faster since October 2025. Anthropic’s policy treats a doubling of progress plausibly driven by automated research as a warning trigger, not proof that a specific danger has arrived. METR’s review of Anthropic’s August risk report concluded that the company’s public account understated both the estimated acceleration and the uncertainty around it. Figures in an internal version implied a rate of 1.97, METR said. Anthropic had the right to redact the review and removed most of the evidence METR considered informative, saying disclosure could help competing developers. METR also said Anthropic halted a planned audit of how it allocates computing resources between capability and safety research, choosing to focus first on risk assessment.

items.title: [theguardian.com] European bomb threats spread to broadcasters as Ireland cites likely campaign
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

Bomb threats spread from flights to broadcasters on Friday, prompting evacuations in Ireland and Bulgaria as aircraft across Europe again received threats. Ireland’s government said the threats were likely part of a coordinated campaign of disruption, but no explosives or injuries were reported in the incidents. The alerts extended a week of hoaxes that have triggered diversions, inspections and fighter-jet escorts. Emails bearing the name “Mikhail Andropov” went to Irish public broadcaster RTÉ and Bulgaria’s Nova TV; British broadcaster Sky also reported a security threat. RTÉ evacuated staff and suspended programming before police cleared its premises. On Friday, a Wizz Air flight from Prague to Rome diverted to Venice, while Hungarian fighter jets escorted three passenger planes through the country’s airspace. Investigators have not identified the sender or established whether the threats to newsrooms and airlines were connected. The European Commission activated an information-sharing mechanism among EU countries, and European security experts are due to meet in Brussels next week to discuss responses. Ireland is also preparing a significant security operation for next week’s European Political Community and EU leaders’ meetings in Dublin.

items.title: [therecord.media] Three men charged in alleged $129 million AI fraud targeting companies
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

Three men have been charged in Manhattan with allegedly using artificial intelligence to impersonate company executives and lawyers and persuade employees to transfer more than $129 million to accounts controlled by the group and co-conspirators. Prosecutors say the alleged scheme ran from July 2024 to February 2026 and targeted thousands of companies worldwide. The defendants, Jacob Soall, Sharon Hazan and Guy Sheetrit, were arrested in Spain and the United Kingdom between June and September 2026. U.S. extradition requests are pending. The indictment describes a two-stage impersonation: someone posing as a CEO asked accounting staff to handle a confidential transaction, then a supposed lawyer reinforced the request and supplied wire instructions. The alleged losses include $11.5 million from a British financial technology company, $5.2 million from a Florida pet-food company and $4.8 million from a Missouri hospital system. Prosecutors say the group moved funds through bank accounts in several countries, converted them into cryptocurrency and distributed the proceeds. The defendants face charges including wire fraud, aggravated identity theft and money laundering; prosecutors say the counts carry a combined maximum sentence of 104 years in prison if they are convicted. Sheetrit’s lawyers said he has no connection to the case and maintains his innocence. Lawyers for Soall and Sheetrit had not responded to the Associated Press when it reported the indictment, and it was unclear whether Hazan had an attorney.

Thailand’s Public Health Ministry warned that a powerful El Niño could worsen PM2.5 pollution across 40 high-risk provinces through May, putting about 16 million vulnerable people at risk. The Pacific El Niño event is expected to intensify toward year-end and continue into early 2027. Vietnam’s government has ordered agencies and local authorities to prepare for related drought, water shortages, saltwater intrusion, wildfire and flooding risks by updating response plans and checking water supplies.

items.title: [dw.com] Netanyahu’s governing bloc leads partial count, but lacks majority
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s governing bloc was projected to win 55 seats after more than half the ballots were counted Wednesday, compared with 49 for the opposition led by former military chief Gadi Eisenkot and 15 for Arab-led parties. The partial count followed Tuesday’s parliamentary election, Israel’s first national vote since the Hamas-led Oct. 7, 2023, attack and the wars that followed. All three groupings remained short of the 61 seats needed for a Knesset majority. Television exit polls initially gave Eisenkot’s bloc a narrow lead, but revised estimates showed the main camps nearly tied. The Central Elections Committee reported turnout of 77.7%, the highest since 1999. Arab-led parties made substantial gains and could influence government formation, although Netanyahu has rejected relying on their support and Eisenkot has also distanced himself from a coalition partnership with them. The remaining ballots include a large batch of special votes, and final results are expected by Nov. 4. Once results are official, President Isaac Herzog will consult party representatives and assign a lawmaker he considers best placed to form a coalition. Talks could take weeks, and another election is possible if no government can be formed.

Pro-Russian groups have claimed responsibility, but those claims are unverified, and the Kremlin denied Russian involvement.

items.title: [helpnetsecurity.com] OpenSSH flaw exploited to access passwordless Alpine Linux accounts
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

Attackers began exploiting an OpenSSH authentication flaw within nine hours of its Nov. 5 disclosure, and security firm Previdian confirmed root access on an Alpine Linux honeypot. Tracked as CVE-2026-123158, the flaw can let an unauthenticated attacker access certain passwordless accounts by submitting an oversized password. It carries a CVSS severity score of 8.1. The vulnerability affects OpenSSH servers on musl-based Linux systems when PAM is disabled, password authentication is enabled, and specific account and password-hash conditions are met. Alpine Linux, OpenWrt, Buildroot and Yocto are among the systems that may be affected; glibc-based distributions such as Debian and Ubuntu are not. OpenSSH released version 10.6p2 on Nov. 5, and Alpine issued patched packages. Administrators must restart sshd after updating; otherwise, the running daemon remains unchanged.

items.title: [news.un.org] UN says record greenhouse gases lock in centuries-long warming
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

The World Meteorological Organization (WMO), the United Nations’ weather agency, reported that atmospheric concentrations of carbon dioxide, methane and nitrous oxide all reached record levels in 2025. Carbon dioxide averaged 426.8 parts per million, methane 1,948 parts per billion and nitrous oxide 339.1 parts per billion—153%, 267% and 126% of pre-industrial levels, respectively. The annual bulletin measures gases accumulated in the atmosphere, not emissions released during the year. About half of annual carbon dioxide emissions remain in the atmosphere. The WMO says the gases’ heat-trapping effect will drive warming for decades or centuries; the past 11 years were the warmest on record. Carbon dioxide rose 2.8 parts per million from 2024 to 2025, below the previous year’s 3.6-ppm increase but still above the decade average of 2.6 ppm. The WMO linked the slower increase partly to recovering land carbon sinks and fewer fire emissions after the 2023-24 El Niño. It warned that concentrations could rise further in 2026 as fossil-fuel use continues and another powerful El Niño affects land sinks. The bulletin will inform negotiators at the Nov. 9-20 COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Türkiye.

Spain’s Council of State, an advisory body, unanimously approved its opinion on a proposed decree regulating data centers, clearing the way for the government to adopt it before the Nov. 29 general election. The council backed the state’s authority to regulate, the use of a royal decree and the urgent procedure, but said the government must make four essential changes before approval. The required revisions include tighter public oversight, clearer sanctions and stronger estimates of compliance costs. The rules aim to manage data centers’ electricity and water use and limit pressure on the power system. The government is expected to submit the revised decree to the Council of Ministers; the opinion does not itself enact the rules.

items.title: [3dprinting.com] 3D-printed tungsten tiles withstand 74 plasma discharges in fusion test
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

Full-size 3D-printed tungsten tiles survived 74 plasma discharges inside the DIII-D National Fusion Facility in San Diego, remaining intact after about four minutes of total plasma exposure over three days. The test subjected industrial-scale printed components to conditions relevant to fusion-reactor hardware, including intense heat and particle bombardment. Researchers from North Carolina State University, Oak Ridge National Laboratory and Japanese manufacturer JEOL made the tiles using electron-beam powder bed fusion, keeping the tungsten powder bed above 1,400°C during printing to limit cracking. The parts still await detailed erosion and surface analysis after a radiation survey.

items.title: [gizmodo.com] Protesters breach Microsoft’s 78-megawatt Amsterdam data center site
items.content_html:
🏔️ ✏️

Protesters breached the construction site of Microsoft’s planned Amsterdam data center Friday, with around 100 people entering the site. Pure Data Centres is developing the facility, which consists of three towers about 85 meters tall with a capacity of 78 megawatts, for Microsoft as its sole tenant. Dutch police said they detained 150 to 200 people, and one officer was slightly injured. AFP reported that construction stopped for the day. Campaigners say the project’s electricity demand could equal that of Amsterdam’s households, a claim not independently established in the reporting, and argue that the development puts pressure on local power and water supplies. Organizers seek a pause on new large-scale facilities until governments set clearer rules, rather than closure of existing data centers. European Union technology chief Henna Virkkunen has argued that Europe needs data centers to develop its own AI capacity, while saying residents must be protected from higher energy bills, blackouts and environmental damage.
